canberra.title: Who was really the villain in Batemans Bay’s great circus lion escape?
canberra.snippet: Picture this: it’s 1907, and the Eroni circus has rolled into Batemans Bay. You’re in the big top tent with 20 per cent of the enti...
canberra.content:
Human interaction with captive lions is seen here with Mademoiselle Scheel pictured in 1905. Photo: The John and Mable Ringling Museum of Art, public domain.

Picture this: it’s 1907, and the Eroni circus has rolled into Batemans Bay. You’re in the big top tent with 20 per cent of the entire town’s population (that’s just 50 people by the way), and an elephant has just manoeuvred a cage of four agitated lions into the ring.

Enclosed in the cage with the grumpy lions is an equally grumpy lion tamer desperately trying to get the lions to perform for the gathered crowd. With minimal luck, the trainer attempts to leave the cage but the entrance is blocked by uncooperative lions, and everything is about to go wrong.

Making for an alternate exit, the ringmaster unlatches the cage for the trainer to escape, and two lionesses sniff freedom. One heads for the big top doors and stops for a snack on some of the circus horses before disappearing into the town.

One of the few surviving images showing the historic Eroni Bros Circus, not to be confused with the modern Eroni Circus which is unrelated. Photo origin: unknown, public domain.

Panic ensues under the big top, and the crowd scatters as three of the lions are secured. What follows is an all-night lion hunt through Batemans Bay.

The hunting party led by Senior Constable Kilfoyle arm themselves with rifles and ammunition from a defunct local rifle club, and more than a dozen men set out in pursuit.

At midnight, local resident Tim Maloney spots the lioness near the Illawarra Steam Navigation Company store and fires at her, missing. Subsequent shots are fired as circus employees and want-to-be big game hunters stalk the lioness through town, all shots missing their target and it’s not until 9 am that she’s spotted snacking on a cow at Little Flat.

Cornered and being fired upon, the lioness charges and lands her target, a Mr Albert Vietch, who finds his arm seized in the jaws of the lioness as he is violently swung around like a rag doll.

If you prefer your tales of adventure to have a happy ending, it’s best to stop reading here.

Lion taming as a profession dates back to the 1820s and was popularised with travelling circuses. Here lion tamer Jack Bonavita wrangles his 500 pound beast. Photo: Hall, public domain.

Mr Vietch is eventually released from the lioness’s grip, and Mr Maloney shoots the lioness through the left eye, the shot being fatal. The pair then split the 20 pound reward with Mr Vietch using his share to pay for his medical bills.

I like to think Mr Maloney used his 10 pounds to shout consecutive rounds of beers at the pub as he recounted the tale of the time he successfully hunted a lion through downtown Batemans Bay, but that detail has been lost to history.

I have recounted this tale as a high adventure, just as nationwide newspapers of the day did, but viewed through a modern lens, it is of course an animal welfare disaster, packed with serious misgivings for public safety and a tragedy for a trapped and abused wild animal.

It wasn’t very long ago that you could still see a lion in a circus here in Australia, with the final exotic animals being retired from Stardust Circus in 2021.

It wasn’t public safety, animal welfare or even a nationwide ban that finally saw Australia’s last six performing lions retire; the RSPCA reported that it was the inability for Stardust to find insurance for the animals.

Aside from insurance, widespread ethics-based council regulations, and public sentiment that sees 85 per cent of people not supporting exotic animals used in this way, there is no government legislation that prevents the use of exotic animals in Australian circuses.

Told the right way, the story of Eroni’s escaped lion is a cracking yarn, one that the passage of time hasn’t dulled, but what time has changed is possibly who is the villain in the story and who is the victim.

Original Article published by Tenele Conway on About Regional.

canberra.title: Parents push to build bike park dream following teen’s sudden death
canberra.snippet: When Tracy and Christian Hall look at the hills around the suburb of Gordon, they think of their son Harrison. The 14-year-old known as H...
canberra.content:
Harry Hall had a passion for biking and a dream to make a difference. Photos: Supplied.

When Tracy and Christian Hall look at the hills around the suburb of Gordon, they think of their son Harrison.

The 14-year-old known as Harry was a mountain biking fanatic and took every chance he could to go on after-school rides and construct jumps in the mountains.

“He saved up, he worked three days a week at the Little Luxton cafe and we matched the money to buy him a brand new Trek,” Harry’s mother Tracy said.

“He slept with it, it was in his room … that’s how much he loved mountain biking.”

Harry and his best mate, Charlie, had a dream to construct their own track in southern Canberra.

But it’s a dream he won’t be able to witness.

Harry with his mate Charlie before tackling the trails at Mogo. Photo: Supplied.

About four weeks ago, the lively teenager caught the flu. After recovering from that, he suffered from a gastro bug.

Once better, he went on a school camp in the Hunter region but the school called to let his parents know he’d been complaining of chest pains.

“He’s an active kid, so it takes a lot for him to not take part in activities,” Harry’s father Christian said.

Tracy and Christian drove to the camp and took Harry to the closest emergency department. It was suggested he may have some leftover inflammation from his illnesses, but he wasn’t getting better.

When he reached Canberra Hospital he was diagnosed with pericarditis, which is swelling and inflammation of the sac that surrounds the heart.

Harry appeared to be responding to treatment, with talks he would soon go home.

But the 14-year-old suffered a cardiac arrest, and his heart couldn’t be restarted because of the pressure from the fluid surrounding the organ.

It was discovered he had a hole in his aorta, which was fixed in surgery, but his brain didn’t survive the lack of oxygen he’d experienced.

“We both knew he was gone,” Christian said.

“For such a fit, young guy … for this to happen – and particularly when we were on a pathway to getting him home – it’s been a complete shock.”

Harry died on 26 September.

Already, Harry’s legacy is living on.

The teenager was Tracy and Christian’s miracle child, conceived after seven years of IVF treatments.

He’s now delivered miracles to other families, saving four people’s lives as he was a registered organ donor.

Now Tracy and Christian want to make his dream of having a mountain biking track in his own backyard come true.

Nature-loving Harry always needed to get outside.

“He’d climb trees, be the first one into the ocean, always taking his shoes off and jumping off rocks,” Tracy said.

“We found, once he’d been able to get out, he’d settle down to do what he actually needed to do.”

Harry with a new bike.

Harry and Charlie had been talking for about a year about the mountain biking track-project, and Harry’s death has spurred his loved ones to take action much sooner than planned.

A GoFundMe has been established to get some funds ready to go, and Brindabella MLA Caitlin Tough has sponsored a petition to make the dream a reality.

It’s hoped the amount raised through the fundraiser – plus the money Tracy and Christian had set aside for Harry’s education – will be matched by the ACT Government, and used to develop a design and even construct the tracks.

“We want to present the cash to the government and say, ‘your turn, let’s make this happen’,” Tracy said.

“Let’s build something decent, just as they did out at Chisholm.”

Tracy and Christian want to create a legacy for Harry in Canberra’s south to give other teenagers access to the joy he experienced on the back of a bike.

There’s a block of land behind the Covenant Christian School where he loved to ride that they already have their eye on.

“His birthday is in November, so we’re already planning to go up to ‘Harry’s Hill’ and do a little something,” Tracy said.

To have something permanent to remember their son by, in the place he loved, would bring something positive to such a tragic event.

“This is such a waste, he was a healthy, bright kid … we don’t want him to have died in vain,” Christian said.

“Something positive has to come out of something so negative.

“To have something named after him, for him to leave a legacy for years to come – that would mean the absolute world to us.”

canberra.title: Be gone, bogongs: Time to get migrating already
canberra.snippet: Let’s go to the South Coast for school holidays, I said. It’ll be fun and relaxing. Lies. It will be a week full of moth swarms, moth car...
canberra.content:
Look at them, plotting how best to infiltrate our fly screens and throw a party on my pillow tonight. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Let’s go to the South Coast for school holidays, I said. It’ll be fun and relaxing.

Lies. It will be a week full of moth swarms, moth carcasses and other moth-related trauma.

Whenever we can, we visit our favourite spot in Bawley Point. The accommodation is simple and immersed in nature, which we usually love. We wake to kangaroos on the doorstep and walk the beach for some whale-spotting and stingrays lapping at our feet. It’s a heavenly place. If you’ve ever read Alison Lester’s Magic Beach, that is the vibe.

What I don’t recall seeing before – in either this iconic Aussie kids book or our real-life destination – is a plague of meddlesome moths.

Right now, these aggravating little brown voyagers are absolutely everywhere.

They’re in my clothes and on my couch. They’re hiding under the dish drying rack. They’re clustered in my shoes.

When I pick up my hat? Moth. Pull some toilet paper? Moth. Unfolding my beach chair? Majestic moth fireworks.

Basically, anything you put down belongs to the moths now.

In last week’s column, I claimed to love animals of all shapes, sizes and species. Well, I would like to rescind that statement.

From the faint flip-flapping of tiny feathery wings to the gross mystery dust they leave in their wake, I have had enough of moths.

And to top it all off, they think they’re so endangered!

Apparently their population has dwindled in recent years, with a catastrophic 99.5 per cent collapse around 2017-19 earning them a spot on the endangered species list.

Senior conservation biologist at Zoos Victoria Marissa Parrott told ABC News: “We are so excited to see the numbers of bogong moths right now, it’s the best year in nearly a decade for them”.

Yes, it’s all very exciting, I say as I pick a moth from my hair.

Dr Parrott told The Guardian: “Every moth is precious, and we want to help them on their migration”.

Well, she’s half right. They can migrate right off.

Last night, I snapped my biscuit with the whole situation. I was properly mothed off.

Armed with what we have termed “the moth glass”, I flew around the bedroom, cackling wildly as I caught every last winged intruder and threw them triumphantly (but gently) out the door.

But apparently the laws of fly screens don’t apply to bloody moths.

Around 3am, I woke to the sound of a moth party.

Like some kind of full moon soiree, the space between the blind and window pane was alive with the doof-doof of tiny shenanigans. The moths – clearly drunk – were dive-bombing repeatedly into the glass, making a surprising amount of racket for a gathering of insects.

Do these moths think they’re better than me?

They think they’re so special and protected. They help themselves to VIP all-areas access. And now they’re having a better holiday than me.

I realise at this point I have fully anthropomorphised these innocent insects. It doesn’t help that some witty corners of the internet have termed these tiny terrorists “Mothew”, giving name to our collective enemy and its many, barely-perceptible faces.

But I cannot deal with this miniscule adversary and their mildly inconvenient presence. And yes, I realise this makes me look less resilient than… well, a bogong moth.

Fortunately, they’re not here to stay. Apparently they are just passing through en route for the Australian Alps. But respectfully, do they know that?

Right now, they don’t seem in a hurry to do anything, other than play an epic, never-ending game of hide and seek.

Dear Mothew, I wish you every success on your trip. But please, get a move on. My sanity is at risk of becoming endangered.

canberra.title: Canberra’s tiny supermarket on the road to nowhere that turned a farm around
canberra.snippet: There are not many reasons to head out on Kambah Pool Road. Dead-ending at a swimming hole on the Murrumbidgee River, for decades it saw ...
canberra.content:
Guy Lilleyman started growing microgreens during lockdown and now sells them alongside the family beef and eggs. Photo: Tenele Conway.

There are not many reasons to head out on Kambah Pool Road. Dead-ending at a swimming hole on the Murrumbidgee River, for decades it saw some summer traffic heading for a cool-down and not much else.

Then in 2018 a fridge popped up. Situated in front of the Lilleyman family property, Amberly Farm, the fridge was stocked to the brim with eggs laid right there on the farm, and over the years it built a cult following of people who swore that once you’d gone Amberly, you wouldn’t be buying any other eggs.

With distribution across a number of outlets in Canberra, including the Fyshwick Fresh Food Markets, Guy Lilleyman, one part of the Lilleyman family farmers spanning two generations, noticed customers were still making the journey to their farm gate, and an idea hatched.

“We were working at the front of the property one day and watching all of the cars pulling in for eggs. The road doesn’t go anywhere, so they were making a special trip just for the eggs, and we saw the opportunity to do something bigger.”

The shipping container-based micro-market was installed in 2024. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Dropping a modified shipping container into place, the Lilleymans set about creating what they call the Amberley Micro-Market, a 7-day-a-week farmers market right at their front gates.

The self-service micro-market is stocked with meat and produce that may have some of the lowest food miles in the region: a 100-metre trip up the driveway.

Restocked daily, you’ll find hormone-free, chemical-free, grass-fed Black Angus beef, an arm of the farm managed by John Lilleyman, the patriarch of the family.

You’ll also find spray-free microgreens, a lockdown project led by Guy Lilleyman. Ma’s Pantry products include kumquat marmalade and Ma’s famous chilli jam. Ma refers to Carol, the matriarch of the Lilleyman family, and then there are the pasture-raised eggs, a project started by Adam Lilleyman, Guy’s brother.

The micro-market has given the Lilleymans an outlet to sell their produce profitably. Photo: Tenele Conway.

“We originally wanted a way to improve the soil, and so we started with 500 hens, but to be a viable business producing eggs, we’ve scaled up to 5000 hens that can roam across 100 acres, and that seems to be the sweet spot,” explains Adam.

Adam laughs that he could write a book of all the things he’s learnt not to do with chickens over the years as he reveals that the Lilleymans were new to farming in 2012, when John and Carol’s retirement project of buying a Kambah cattle farm got out of hand.

Pasture-raised Amberly Farm eggs are what the Lilleymans are best known for in the region. Photo: Tenele Conway.

It’s an unusual way to get into the game, with John’s background in software engineering providing minimal experience in rearing cattle. Turns out it’s a path all the Lilleymans followed, with Guy explaining that he’s actually a musician as he stands in his heated tent, running his fingers through his mizuna and pea shoots.

In addition to his microgreens, Guy heads up the micro-market project, explaining that the tiny shop, which not only stocks their produce but also produce from like-minded businesses from around the region, has been a turning point for the family farming business, allowing them to tap into direct-to-consumer sales, lowering their cost of sale enough to finally make the farming financially viable.

“100 per cent of our eggs are now sold through the micro-market; not having to sell them at wholesale prices has been a game-changer,” Guy explains.

With the micro-market running smoothly, the family is now seeking approval to run farm tours, and if you ever get the chance to set foot on Amberly Farm, it’s well worth your time.

If emotions can be attributed to chickens, these are the happiest you’ll find. The chicken pre-school, as Guy refers to the training paddock for new arrivals, is an amusing procession of chickens learning to do chickeny things like perching.

The Maremma dogs stand nearby guarding their individual flocks with the seriousness of the Royal residence security at Buckingham Palace. The automated egg-weighing apparatus is a Wonka-esque machine that separates the light from the heavy, and the humid microgreens tent shows that small ideas can feed a neighbourhood.

Until that tourism project finds its feet, pop by the micro-market; there’s plenty of inspiration for dinner.

The Amberly Micro-Market is at 325 Kambah Pool Rd, Kambah. It’s open from 7:30 am to 7:30 pm, 365 days a year.

canberra.title: Did you spot Joe Rider? If not, you missed a vulnerable road user
canberra.snippet: Canberran Jen Woods has spent the last 25-odd years relishing the freedom of riding a motorcycle across the country. “It’s a ...
canberra.content:
Motorcycle riders have been wearing high-vis ‘Joe’ vests to make Canberra motorists extra aware of their presence. Photo: MRA ACT.

Canberran Jen Woods has spent the last 25-odd years relishing the freedom of riding a motorcycle across the country.

“It’s a wonderful way to travel … just being out there and among what’s happening, more so than if you’re in a car,” she said.

“You smell the smells and feel the weather; it just feels so good.”

But the 70-something-year-old, who is also the Motorcycle Riders Association ACT president, is also very aware that she’s considered a vulnerable road user.

Motorcyclists make up just 5 per cent of registered vehicles in the ACT, but about 44 per cent of Canberra’s road deaths in the past two years have been motorcycle riders.

Nearly one-third of people admitted to hospital following crashes in the past two years have also been motorcyclists.

The federal government’s Road Trauma Australia report showed this is a national trend: motorcycle fatalities have experienced the sharpest rise of any road user group in the country over the past four years.

October is Motorcycle Awareness Month, and so riders donned high-visibility vests for the first week of the month to represent ‘Joe Rider’.

It’s a test for other road users to see if they’re really aware of motorcyclists in Canberra, and to consider how they’re interacting with motorbikes.

“If we can get people actually seeing them, hopefully we can change driver behaviour,” Ms Woods said.

“Don’t play chicken, don’t tailgate a motorcycle – it’s a fairly terrifying thing … it can take your power away and make you feel quite vulnerable.”

Ms Woods was aware that motorcyclists have a bad rap, with most people probably picturing a 20-something ducking and weaving through traffic for the thrill of it.

She wanted to remind all drivers that, under the helmet, that’s someone’s friend, child, grandparent, co-worker, all wanting to get home safe too.

“I’d say about 99 per cent of us are just people; we’re not anything bad,” Ms Woods said.

“Please, consider us, look for us, see us.”

The ACT Government is currently working on its ACT Road Safety Framework 2026-2031, and has committed to Vision Zero.

Ms Woods said that, along with motorists’ awareness, serious work was needed on how roads kept everyone safe.

“[For example] pothole repairs need to be done properly so they’re not just washed away when the next rain comes,” she said.

“Oil spills must be cleaned up properly, not just have sand put down and left there.

“We would also like to see more road hazard signs to warn people [of incidents ahead], and have them monitored and removed when the hazard’s gone, so they don’t become meaningless.”

She also took issue with comparisons made between ACT motorcycle injuries and deaths to NSW, as if the higher statistics in NSW meant the ACT was a safer place to ride.

“It’s not really comparing apples to apples,” Ms Woods said.

“NSW has long country roads, and the ACT doesn’t have the same amount of heavy traffic.”

“Road safety strategies are failing … and failing on all fronts.”

The ACT Government is using October to encourage all motorcycle riders to adopt a defensive riding mindset and asked all road users to stay alert, anticipate hazards and make safe decisions every time they travel.

“Unlike drivers, riders have very little physical protection in a crash, increasing their risk of serious injury,” City and Environment Directorate policy, legislation and housing executive branch manager Dr Su Wild-River said.

“Staying alert and making safe choices can help reduce the risk of crashes and serious injuries.”

Motorcycle riders are encouraged to ride defensively, including adjusting their speed to suit road, weather and traffic conditions, taking corners safely, approaching intersections with caution and only overtaking when it is safe to do so. Riders should also wear appropriate protective gear and ensure their motorcycle is roadworthy before every ride.

Drivers are reminded to look twice for motorcycles and check their blind spots before changing lanes, merging or entering traffic. Using indicators before turning or changing lanes, giving riders plenty of space and avoiding tailgating can help reduce the risk of crashes.

Plus, everyone should follow the road rules and only overtake when it is safe and legal to do so.

For Ms Woods, it’s also about remembering no one is invincible.

“The road is a shared space … there’s a responsibility for all of us when we get behind the wheel,” she said.

“It has to be every person looking out for motorcyclists, just as we look out for pedestrians and other road users.”

australia.title: Missing Australian hiker Jordan Yap last seen on remote trail found dead in Peru
australia.snippet: Family and friends say Melbourne man should be remembered for ‘immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives’ Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
An Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said.

Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.

In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.

“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.

“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.

“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”

The Melbourne man was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker.

His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco.

The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.

A spokesperson from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian who had died in Peru.

“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said.

- with AAP

australia.title: A Trump impersonator and opera singers: CPAC was a spectacle, but the right still can’t agree how to take down Labor
australia.snippet: Preferences proved the sticking point at the conference as conservatives face the prospect of a third successive election defeat Get our ...
australia.content:
Many mainstream Australians would feel as if they’d been dropped in a foreign country at the Conservative Political Action Conference, lost amid oblique references to transgender swimmers, blue hair, women’s bathrooms, jokes about falling off stages and Matt Canavan in hi-vis and speed dealer sunnies.

It’s an interesting spectacle. At this year’s conference in Brisbane, rightwing campaigner Monica Smit was deep in conversation with a Donald Trump impersonator, opera singers belted out the national anthem (the first verse, twice, for unknown reasons), senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and her folk singer husband sang the anthem again, and Karl Stefanovic jokingly thanking CPAC for “rudely interrupting my unemployment”.

Stickers depicting Albanese with a Pinocchio nose, holding a brown burlap sack and a large blue sex toy emblazoned with “United Nations global citizen award” were found in the conference hall and in the men’s urinals. They carried no authorisation message, and did not appear to be officially endorsed by CPAC. Journalists were asked to wear a large red media accreditation lanyard emblazoned with “FAKE NEWS” – a gag CPAC has been pulling for years.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

There was Barnaby Joyce handing out a few notes as props during his free-wheeling lecture about the value of money and the historical silver content of Roman coins, and seemingly every One Nation figure with a public profile (besides Farrer MP David Farley) wandering the halls.

Alongside boilerplate rightwing chaff like lower taxes, fiscal discipline and welfare, CPAC is a hotbed for hyper-engaged conservatives riled up on the red cordial of Sky After Dark. Last year’s event featured speakers criticising Peter Dutton as “Labor-lite”.

For all the twisting rabbit holes which various speeches followed, there was only really one prevailing theme which most boiled down to, and which this year’s conference revolved around.

Preferences.

To put it more accurately, the conference was about how Australia’s conservative right planned to boot Albanese and Labor out of office at the next election. With 94 Labor seats, and a splintered rightwing vote with Angus Taylor’s diminished Coalition opposition being whacked by Pauline Hanson’s surging One Nation, it’s a tall task.

To attend this year’s CPAC was to see Australia’s right recognising in real-time that they needed to figure out a way to cooperate; that for all the mocking of Albanese Labor as allegedly “the worst government in history”, conservatives face a third successive election defeat.

CPAC, in messages to attenders, identified what it saw as the problem: “If you support One Nation but won’t preference the Coalition, or support the Coalition but won’t preference One Nation, you risk reinstalling Labor.”

But identifying the problem is only half the challenge. By the conference’s end, it wasn’t clear how parties of the right would, or could, cooperate. While Hanson signed a pledge to “to work together”, challenging Taylor and Canavan to follow suit, it came hours after she’d told the conference they shouldn’t trust the Coalition, and appeared to call the Liberal leader a “smarmy management consultant” unfit to replace Albanese.

Hanson at CPAC 2025 said she would “no longer be the bridesmaid” to the Coalition. She seems wedded to that, and said the ball was in Taylor’s court as to how their two parties would coexist.

Taylor had earlier dodged questions from Karl Stefanovic – to boos from the audience – about how the Coalition should cooperate with One Nation. He tried burnishing his conservative credentials by apologising for net zero, pandemic spending and immigration increases under Coalition governments, and later claiming “I know how to get Australia out of the hole Labor has put us in”, but it was clear many here had only come to see the Hanson show.

In previous years, the mood at the conference has been a decent weathervane indicating where the wind of the right is blowing.

In 2022, CPAC’s prevailing theme was urging the opposition to oppose the Indigenous voice referendum; a month later, the Nationals did, later followed by the Liberals. In 2025, alarmed Coalition speakers begged attenders for their loyalty in the face of One Nation’s rise, culture warriors railed against Sussan Ley’s leadership, and Canavan said the Liberals were on “the cusp” of dropping net zero. Within months, the Coalition split again, the Liberals dumped net zero and then Ley, and Hanson’s surge continued.

There’s some way to go before the next election, due by May 2028. The conservative side of politics still lays splintered. We’ll look back on this weekend to see if it was the start of the right’s rebuild, or just another forum to bag the prime minister.

australia.title: Ben Roberts-Smith attends Canberra event honouring Australian troops who served in Afghanistan
australia.snippet: Anthony Albanese speaks at Australian War Memorial event commemorating 25th anniversary of country’s involvement in the conflict Get our ...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese has honoured Australian troops who served in Afghanistan, using the 25th anniversary of the country’s involvement in the conflict to describe their heroism as a fight for “who we are as a people”.

The prime minister joined hundreds of veterans, family members and dignitaries at a commemoration of the start of the campaign in Canberra on Sunday, with nation’s most decorated living soldier and accused war criminal Ben Roberts-Smith among the crowd at the Australian War Memorial.

“In New York, fires were still burning at Ground Zero from the September 11 attacks a month earlier. The world felt upended,” Albanese said of the start of Operation Slipper.

“Though it would change so devastatingly a year later in Bali, it was not yet directly our fight.

“Yet Australia did what is so resolutely in our nature. We went to support our friend and ally.

“We went because we saw what was at stake, and we went on the principle that September 11 was an attack on a way of life that belonged just as much to us.”

He said the more than 35,000 defence force members deployed over the following two decades did so because the very freedoms “that are at the heart of who we are as a people and a nation were under threat”.

Roberts-Smith, who denies the allegations against him, attended the event alongside family members and supporters, as well as former prime ministers John Howard, Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison.

The governor general, Sam Mostyn, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, were also present in the bright sunshine.

Roberts-Smith was awarded Australia’s highest military honour – the Victoria Cross – for his service in Afghanistan, but now faces accusations he murdered five unarmed detainees during his deployment.

The former Special Air Service regiment corporal sat alongside his partner, Sarah Matulin, after a judge agreed to vary his bail conditions to allow him to visit Canberra.

Deployments to the Middle East continued until withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021.

US troops left a few months later after signing an agreement with the Taliban, who swiftly returned to power and reintroduced authoritarian control, including strict suppression of women and girls’ rights.

Some 47 Australian personnel died as a result of their service and 263 were wounded, while thousands more allied soldiers were killed.

Tens of thousands of civilians were also estimated to have been killed during the war.

Despite the controversy over Australia’s military involvement in Afghanistan and its legacy, the troops who served on the ground remain intensely proud of what they achieved.

Soldier Mathew Bell was deployed in 2012, aged 24, with his infantry battalion to a forward operating base in Afghanistan’s “badlands” west of Tarinkot.

More than a decade after he returned to Australia, Bell remembers his unit’s work with a sense of honour and accomplishment.

“We changed that little part of Afghanistan, that little part of the world for good,” the former lance corporal, now 38, said.

Bell said girls were able to attend school, medical services were rolled out to villages and “there was freedom”.

“Not the oppression we’re seeing now under the Taliban government,” the father of two said.

“Our role was essentially to go out on either vehicle-mounted patrols or foot patrols, out among the local population through the desert, through the green zone, keeping the Taliban at bay.

“It was a hot area. Once you stepped over that line in the sand, like, that was Taliban territory.”

One of Bell’s close mates was badly wounded in a roadside bomb explosion and on more than one occasion, his section was pinned down by sniper fire.

Services were also held at the Anzac Memorial in Sydney’s Hyde Park, at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance and other sites around the country.

Australians who served in the Afghanistan War were deployed in various roles and missions contributing to reconstruction efforts, democratic governance, training and humanitarian aid.

Operation Slipper was followed between 2015 and 2021 by Operation Highroad and the Kabul airlift in August 2021.

australia.title: Two Carlton players treated in hospital after off-season night out
australia.snippet: Club issues brief statement about Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, saying latter suffered minor cut to head after a fall An off-season nigh...
australia.content:
An off-season night out for Carlton football club teammates ended with two players admitted to hospital for treatment on Sunday morning, in what the club says are “separate circumstances”.

The club released a statement on Sunday confirming that AFL players Lachie Cowan, 21, and Will Hayward, 27, had been treated and discharged, after reports in several media outlets about the aftermath of an off-season night out.

Guardian Australia understands both players were both part of a larger group that had been socialising on Saturday evening.

The club statement said Cowan had “received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later” but did not provide any more information about the circumstances.

Hayward was also admitted to hospital later on Sunday morning, after returning home.

“Will Hayward experienced a minor cut to the head after a fall, and admitted himself to hospital where he received stitches before being discharged,” Carlton said.

Neither player is understood to be seriously unwell or hurt.

“The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances.”

Ambulance Victoria said paramedics responded to an incident at inner-suburban South Yarra at about 5.15am on Sunday.

A man in his 20s was taken by ambulance to the Alfred hospital in stable condition, Ambulance Victoria said.

AFL players throughout the league are on leave as trade period rolls on until Wednesday night.

australia.title: Parents are being crushed by childcare fees. Will Labor ever deliver a universal system?
australia.snippet: Labor is running out of time to make its case to Australian families about how it is going to make childcare accessible and affordable fo...
australia.content:
Rachel Hill, a mother of two from Sydney, explains the maths of family planning.

The not-for-profit worker has bumped up her workload from two days a week to full-time to try to cover ever-rising costs. Instead, the additional money has been swallowed by childcare fees.

“I did not want to go back full-time, it was purely because of the cost of living,” she says.

“We went from paying around $175 a week for four days of care … to now paying $536 a week for five days, so any increase I got in my salary I’m basically now paying in day care.”

Hill says her husband always wanted a bigger family. If raising children were more affordable, they may have considered having a third. But with only a small village around them, she says “it’s just not working”.

“If our circumstances were different I might have had more reason to pursue more children, but financially it just wasn’t ever going to work for us.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, wants universal childcare to be his political legacy, his entry to the Labor hall of fame alongside Medicare and the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It should, he says, be “as natural as public school”.

But the sector has been rocked by widespread allegations of child abuse and safety breaches, damaging public trust and forcing the government to tighten standards – all while trying to figure out what a universal system might look like and how to pay for it.

It is working against a ticking clock: the 2026 intergenerational report, released last month, showed deaths would outnumber births in Australia by the 2060s. Australia needs more babies, and Labor says universal childcare is key to making that happen.

What is universal childcare?

While many might presume universal childcare means free childcare – akin to public schools for older children – the government has defined it as care that is “available, quality and affordable”. Overseas examples point to provinces in Canada which offer $10 a day capped care, or Estonia, where fees are capped at low weekly or monthly rates tied to the minimum wage. Labor won’t yet say which model it would choose but has indicated it is likely to be means-tested.

It has commissioned two consulting firms to produce separate work outlining the scope of the challenge. The biggest report is by Deloitte and aims to set out the cost of delivering childcare services in any part of the country – metropolitan, outer-suburban, regional or remote.

The work requires the cooperation of about 1,000 childcare centres across that geographic spread but they have not been forthcoming. The low turnout of volunteers has led to the government compelling service providers to hand over the centres’ financial data. Deloitte is due to hand the report to government by the end of the year.

The cabinet is also mulling over a report by KPMG which outlined the business case for the government owning and leasing childcare centres. The work – which the government has refused to release, citing cabinet in confidence rules – centres around the $1bn building early education fund, which provides for state governments and not-for-profits to set up centres in childcare deserts.

The first grant round from that fund was announced this month, with $17.3m split between three not-for-profit providers to build four childcare centres in outer metropolitan and regional areas. Dozens more are yet to be announced.

It gives us a clear hint of where Labor believes it can make a mark. The government wants to see not-for-profits making up a bigger share of the childcare sector, with 70% of the sector currently privately run.

“Outer suburbs and regions where there are growing families, but not enough childcare places, we want to build more quality, not-for-profit early learning in those places that need it the most, and it is part of our journey towards universal early education,” the childcare minister, Jess Walsh, told Guardian Australia.

That shift is starting to happen. In August, the for-profit provider Edge Early Learning went into administration, while competitor G8 has closed dozens of under-enrolled and underperforming centres. This week, Goodstart Early Learning, a not-for-profit provider and one of the recipients of the building early education fund, signed an agreement to investigate the potential take over of up to 31 of Edge Early Learning’s 64 centres.

Goodstart’s head of advocacy, John Cherry, says there is “certainly an opportunity there for the not-for-profit sector to expand, but at the moment, not-for-profit providers around the country are running on very thin margins and very challenged by operational conditions”.

Not-for-profit childcare providers are not necessarily cheaper for parents – comparison website childcare estimator says fees are about 8% cheaper at some not-for-profits – but they consistently have higher quality and safety ratings.

Changing the subsidy

Any reform would also have to tackle the childcare subsidy.

A family with one child and a household income of up to $88,520 now receives a government subsidy covering 90% of childcare fees. That subsidy tapers off at a rate of 1% per additional $5,000 of income, running down to nothing when the household income reaches $538,520.

Labor has consistently raised these subsidies since it came to power in 2022 and says a family with a household income of $168,000, with one child in care for 30 hours a week, is $7,440 a year better off than they would be without the higher subsidies. But the fees themselves have been rising quickly, jumping 7.3% in the 12 months to August – more than twice the inflation rate.

The childcare subsidy was projected to cost the budget about $16.2bn last financial year and is slated to rise to $18.4bn by 2028-29.

The government already has a blueprint for universal childcare sitting on its desk. In June 2024, the productivity commission looked at three options: the recommended option was free childcare for families with a household income under $90,000, then progressively dropping the subsidy down from 100% towards zero with every $5,000 increase in household income, tapering off at $580,000. For a household income of $168,000, mentioned above, that would be an 85% subsidy.

The Productivity Commission also modelled a flat $10 a day or 90% subsidy option for all families but said the cost to the budget would be much higher and the benefit would disproportionately go to wealthier households.

Parents have to wait until their children turn three to get further relief, when additional subsidies offered by state governments for preschool kick in. But preschools run on school terms and typically offer 15 hours a week, leaving considerable gaps for parents working full-time.

The fees now faced by parents are comparable to private school fees, says Eshanee Collins, a Sydney-based mortgage broker. She says returning to work was part of her identity after having children but the cost of care made it a tough decision.

“I work full-time, and in all honesty, our household would probably be better off if I didn’t work and [did] not pay that [childcare] money,” she says.

Childcare is likely to become a key election battleground, with the Coalition looking at both the design of the childcare subsidy and paid parental leave settings, while One Nation has promoted income splitting and other policies that incentivise one parent staying home.

The Greens, meanwhile, have commissioned parliamentary budget office modelling on the cost of providing 50 hours a week of free childcare, which could cost $127bn over a decade.

Whichever way it’s sliced, childcare is expensive to run and public buy-in is essential. Labor is running out of time to decide what model of universal care it wants to pursue – and how to get voters on board.

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

world.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
world.snippet: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding Isaias has become the f...
world.content:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

world.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
world.snippet: Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian journalists...
world.content:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

world.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
world.snippet: Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme A survey of the world’s ...
world.content:
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.

“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”
